audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Douglas 1981:206-207, sec. 2.1.4) is present verbatim in the full-text file we hold, including the sentence truncated in the record ('In words of more than four syllables, secondary stress falls on the penultimate'); the record's evidence note ('search snippets only', 'not re-opened') can be upgraded to full-text-confirmed against the open-access ANU PDF. (2) The stress placement coded per word length as 10 110 1010 10010 100010 (1 = a stressed syllable) is a faithful literal rendering of Douglas: initial primary; secondary on syllable 2 in trisyllables, syllable 3 in quadrisyllables, penult in longer words. The contra note against StressTyp2 (which has 100 for trisyllables) is correctly stated. Caveat worth carrying: the trisyllabic 110 implies adjacent primary+secondary stress, which is unusual for a Pama-Nyungan language and rests on one impressionistic sentence with no stress-marked examples in the cha

sources.note: Only modern first-hand description (Marmion has worked on Wajarri since the 1990s); our classification rests on Douglas 1981's four-sentence impressionistic statement, whose trisyllable claim (secondary stress on syllable 2, i.e. a 1-2 clash, coded 110) is typologically odd and is exactly where StressTyp2 departed from the source (100). A 2023 phonology paragraph would settle 110 vs 100 vs alternating 101.
